newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's interior minister blasts Chechen peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia's interior minister blasts Chechen peace deal.

text.p: Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, renewing his assault on Alexander Lebed's peace deal in breakaway Chechnya, said on Monday the ceasefire was undermining Russia's ability to restore order in the breakaway republic.

Kulikov, a fierce critic of Lebed's August 31 deal with the Chechen separatists, went on the offensive as his rival embarked on his first ever trip to the West as the guest of NATO headquarters in Brussels.
"Peace is a long way off and both politicians and the military will have to fight hard to secure it," said Kulikov. "There is no real calm in Chechnya right now."

Under Lebed's deal Russian troops, which failed to establish control over Chechnya in 21 months of bloody fighting, started withdrawing from the region last month. A decision on whether Chechnya would become independent was deferred for five years.

Last week Kulikov, seen by Lebed as one of the architects of the conflict, drew loud applause in the State Duma (lower house of parliament) when he described the peace deal as a humiliating step towards the disintegration of Russia.

He said on Monday some parties had deliberately exaggerated the numbers of people killed in the conflict, which he put at around 18,500. Estimates that put the figure as high as 100,000 were "a conscious lie with far-reaching aims", he added.

Lebed, a reserve paratroop general who became secretary of the policy-making Security Council in June, told the Duma last week that up to 100,000 people perished in the Chechen conflict and he has said that Kulikov should quit.

Lebed has said he is sure the deal improves the chances of keeping Chechnya as part of Russia. President Boris Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, said Lebed had carried out his instructions to end the war promptly.
On Monday Kulikov repeated his claims that the Chechens were violating the peace agreement.

He said 139 people have been killed in the region since August despite the truce. Rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev had failed to disarm his supporters and was calling up young men, some of whom were being trained in nearby Moslem countries.
Kulikov said it was impossible for his ministry to perform its duties while the Chechens were setting up "a medieval criminal code which allows them to stone people or cut off their arms or legs".
The Chechens have introduced elements of Islamic law in the region, but there have been no reports of judicial amputations.
